question: What is the main goal when treating a patient with a peptic ulcer?

options.A: Heal the ulcer and relieve pain

explanation: We want to help the stomach sore heal up so the patient feels comfortable again and doesn't keep getting painful flare-ups! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h1)

question: Peptic ulcer treatment usually focuses on balancing which two opposing forces in the stomach?

options.A: Red blood cell counts and white blood cell counts
options.B: Dietary sugar intake and physical exercise levels
options.C: Fluid intake and urinary output volume
options.D: Aggressive acid factors and defensive mucosal factors

explanation: Think of it as a tug-of-war! Strong acid tries to damage the stomach, while the stomach's natural mucus tries to protect it. Drugs help restore that balance. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h1)

question: How do Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) mostly stop stomach acid?

options.A: Neutralizing existing acid directly inside the stomach lumen
options.B: Blocking the hydrogen-potassium enzyme pump in parietal cells
options.C: Coating the ulcer base with a thick protective physical paste
options.D: Killing the bacteria responsible for stomach lining infections

explanation: PPIs target the exact tiny pumps in the stomach lining that push acid out. Turn off the pump, and acid production slows right down! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h2)

question: What important tip should you give a patient taking a delayed-release PPI capsule?

options.A: Swallow the capsule whole without chewing or crushing it
options.B: Chew the capsule thoroughly before swallowing with water
options.C: Dissolve the capsule completely in warm lemon juice first
options.D: Open the capsule and mix the powder directly into milk

explanation: Those capsules have a special coating to protect the medicine from stomach acid until it gets where it needs to be. Chewing ruins that protection! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h2)

question: What is the main job of H2-receptor blockers in the stomach?

options.A: Stimulating bicarbonate production in the pancreas
options.B: Blocking histamine to reduce gastric acid secretion
options.C: Coating the entire stomach wall with a protective gel
options.D: Destroying Helicobacter pylori bacterial cell walls

explanation: H2 blockers stop histamine (which usually tells the stomach to make acid) from doing its job, keeping acid levels low. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why must nurses be careful when giving cimetidine to patients taking many other drugs?

options.A: It completely stops the liver from filtering blood entirely
options.B: It immediately destroys all other oral medications in transit
options.C: It causes severe allergic skin rashes in every patient
options.D: It is known to cause many drug interactions in the body

explanation: Cimetidine interacts with liver enzymes, which can change how other medications are processed in the body. Always double-check drug guides! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h3)

question: How do standard antacids give quick relief from heartburn and ulcers?

options.A: Chemically neutralizing existing acid in the stomach
options.B: Creating a physical barrier over the ulcer crater
options.C: Killing the bacteria that cause stomach ulcers
options.D: Stopping parietal cells from manufacturing new acid

explanation: Antacids act like a chemical sponge, directly neutralizing the acid that is already sitting in the stomach and causing that burning feeling. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h4)

question: Which common side effect should you watch out for in patients taking lots of aluminum-based antacids?
explanation: Aluminum has a way of slowing things down in the GI tract, so patients often complain of constipation. Good to keep in mind for nursing care! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h4)

question: How does sucralfate protect an ulcer in the stomach?

options.A: Binding to ulcer craters to form a protective physical barrier
options.B: Neutralizing stomach acid directly through chemical reactions
options.C: Shutting down the proton pumps inside gastric parietal cells
options.D: Stopping histamine release from local immune system cells

explanation: Sucralfate turns into a sticky, protective paste when it hits stomach acid, gluing itself right over the sore like a Band-Aid! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h5)

question: Your patient is prescribed sucralfate along with other oral medications. How should you time their doses?

options.A: Give sucralfate immediately after meals alongside all other pills
options.B: Mix all drugs into the same liquid suspension for convenience
options.C: Crush all medications together and administer them simultaneously
options.D: Separate sucralfate and other oral drugs by at least two hours

explanation: Because sucralfate forms a sticky coating, it can trap other drugs and stop your body from absorbing them. Give other meds a 2-hour window! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why are antibiotics prescribed as part of treatment for some peptic ulcers?

options.A: Directly neutralizing excess hydrochloric acid in the gut
options.B: Blocking histamine receptors on gastric parietal cells
options.C: Coating the stomach wall to prevent physical irritation

explanation: Many ulcers are caused by a stubborn bacteria called H. pylori. Clearing it out with antibiotics helps the ulcer heal completely. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h6)

question: Why do doctors usually prescribe a mix of two different antibiotics for H. pylori instead of just one?

options.A: To prevent the bacteria from developing drug resistance
options.B: To make the treatment cheaper and easier to manufacture
options.C: To eliminate the need for taking any acid-reducing drugs
options.D: To speed up the physical digestion of meals in the stomach

explanation: Using a combination team of antibiotics ensures the bacteria get knocked out completely without learning how to fight off the medicine. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h6)

question: Which common group of over-the-counter pain relievers is a major cause of peptic ulcers?
explanation: NSAIDs like ibuprofen block protective chemicals in the stomach lining, making it super easy for acid to cause damage. [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h7)

question: What lifestyle habit should you strongly advise a patient with peptic ulcer disease to give up?
explanation: Nicotine slows down how fast ulcers heal and makes them way more likely to come back. Encouraging smoking cessation is a great nursing intervention! [learn more](GNS223_U3_T1#GNS223_U3_T1_h7)
